questions.q: What does declaring an ABI array with `as const` enable that a plain `abi: Abi` typed array does not?
options: The compiler can narrow `functionName` to only the real names in that ABI and infer args/return types from it
It converts the ABI into a bigint
It makes the contract call run faster at runtime
It automatically deploys the contract
questions.explain: `as const` locks the ABI to its exact literal type, which lets tools like viem read it function-by-function and narrow functionName, args, and the return type — a plain Abi-typed array only checks shape, not which calls are valid.

questions.q: In the lesson's typed `getTokenBalance` wrapper, what happens if a caller passes a plain string where the `Address` parameter is expected?
options: It silently works exactly the same way
It fails to compile, because Address is a distinct branded/aliased type from plain string
It throws a runtime-only error with no compile-time warning
TypeScript automatically converts the string to an Address
questions.explain: Because the parameter is typed as the project's Address type rather than plain string, passing an untyped string produces a compile error, catching the mistake before runtime.

questions.q: In the Result<T> discriminated union `{ ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: string }`, what is the `ok` field's role?
options: It has no effect on typing, purely cosmetic
It must always be set to true
It's the discriminant/tag that lets TypeScript narrow which other fields exist in each branch
It converts the Result into a Promise
questions.explain: `ok` is the discriminant field — checking `if (result.ok)` narrows the type so `value` is known to exist in that branch, and `error` in the other, which is exactly what makes it a discriminated union.

questions.q: Why might a project prefer a Result<T> return type over simply throwing an exception on a failed contract read?
options: Because exceptions are not supported in TypeScript
Because Result<T> runs the contract call twice for safety
Because throwing is slower than returning an object
Because it's easy for a caller to forget a try/catch, while Result<T> makes the failure case part of the type signature the compiler enforces
questions.explain: Exceptions are easy to forget to handle; encoding success/failure directly in the return type means the compiler can require the caller to check `result.ok` before accessing `value`.

questions.q: What category of production bug does stacking as-const ABIs, typed wrapper functions, and Result<T> together help prevent, according to the lesson?
options: Slow network connections to the RPC provider
Calling a nonexistent function name, passing a wrong argument type, or forgetting to handle a reverted/failed call — all become compile-time errors
Gas price volatility
Smart contract compiler version mismatches
questions.explain: The lesson's point is that combining these three patterns turns typo'd function names, wrong argument types, and unhandled failures into compile-time errors instead of runtime incidents.
